E001.text:
The boat was purchased from Joe Martinez III of San Antonio on December 1st 1994. Lester
Ducote went with me to San Antonio to close the sale and haul the boat, "Knock Down" to Austin. Bill Peace went with me to haul the boat to Port Aransas December 15th.

Arrangements were made with Dumas Marine for compounding, waxing, bottom paint, teak work, etc. Island Boat Works handled the electronic tune up and the installation of trim tabs, Lowrance 350 GPS, washdown, etc. Many short runs up Lydia Ann Waterway or toward Corpus Christi were made during this shakedown period.
E001.note: From conversations with Captain Eddie it sounds like there were a few shakedown runs also made on Lake Austin. Got to find out more about that, it's wild to picture the Seahawk running up the lake towards Pennybacker at 35 knots. John Price was the owner of Island Boat Works. The Lowrance GPS unit he had on board was pretty state of the art at the time.

E004.text: Bill Hudspeth and Val England of Austin Trust Company joined Mike and I for a great snapper trip. We went 80 degrees off the bar to Big Red in 21 fathoms. We used cut squid, giant squid that we bought at the seafood marine shop on the Port Aransas Pass Road going to Port Aransas. They had a big sign out that they had giant, as they called them, and God, they were. So we cut those things up, used them for bait, and caught two really large sow snapper, 24 pounds and 20 pounds, and another 20 or so smaller ones. Beautiful weather, no seas, light north winds. Average speed out and back was 25 knots.
E004.note:
Ed: I’ll say right here, there were no limits in those days on snapper or kingfish, for that matter. They later put three or four, whatever it was, on per day. When we first started down there in earlier boats, we’d bring home 300, 350 pounds a day when we got into them.

Big Red an oil platform painted in red primer paint. I'm curious what the navigational reference of 80 degrees off the bar means.

E-9b5808e48b.text:
Bill Hudspeth, Mike Fleming & I fish a rig located at N27°53.152, W96°44.725. Mike caught a big king - weight unknown, but he  was 55 inches long and had a 24 inch girth. 2 other 15 pound kings, then Mike caught an atlantic sharpnose. That made his trip! He loves sharks.

Wind ENE 15 knots. Rough but lots of sunshine. Good time!

E-8dd394a776.text: Wind still Howling - got out Saturday with Frank Niendorf, sons Davis and Will and of course Lt. Mike Fleming. Went back to above noted rig - caught one shark - missed two others. Seas got to 6-8' so we came in.
E-8dd394a776.note:
Michael had a really big blacktip shark on that I would say would be 75 to 100 pounds. I was working the boat. I asked Frank to gaff, and it turned out he didn’t have much experience as I thought he did. Missed the gaff and grazed the shark, which really put him in high gear. He took off, broke the line, and Michael Fleming was most upset.

The next morning, when I went down to the dock early to get the boat ready, there was a note taped on the console of the Seahawk in Michael’s fine St. Andrew’s hand, and it said:
No more people on this boat that don’t know how to gaff.

Now, not good grammar, but it sure got his feelings [across?]. Michael will always tell you what he thinks and feels, which is great. He was right. We try to cull our people and make sure we have people on board that can handle skill positions like that.

E-77f97f0ab3.text: Too rough for us to take the Seahawk out so Mike and I go out on the Wharf Cat. Rough seas. Mike wins pot of $51 with a 12lb King! Maybe sometime this summer the wind will stop!
E-77f97f0ab3.note:
Ed: The Wharf Cat is still there, I think. We call it the Barf Cat because they get tons of tourists on there and they go out rough. They don’t care how rough it is. They go out. Used to charge ten dollars a head per day when this thing was written.

And you can be, and I’ve seen it where you think, gee, there’s nobody on deck. You don’t see any heads or anybody out on the side because they’re all on the deck throwing up on each other. Great to fish around them because with vomit and all, they chummed in a lot of fish and there's shade under there, so it’s always a good place to catch a ling.

E-f80d412081.text: Bill Hudspeth, Mike & I fish Scorpion Rig - we catch two king and three shark, in one hour.
E-f80d412081.note: Scorpion Rig had two big cranes coming off the sides, looked like one was its tail and one was its head.

E-aabe25e19a.text:
First day of the Port Aransas Deep Sea Tournament. Gary Einkauf, me, Lester, and Alex and Michael head out in six-foot seas to just short of Big Red. Squall makes us decide to head north-northwest to Mighty Whitey and inshore rigs.

We catch a 33-pounder. Lester caught that one. Alex caught a 27-pounder and a 22-pounder that Mike caught. And Mike and Alex were one and two in the junior division at the end of day one with their nice kingfish.
E-aabe25e19a.note: Dad says this was a rough day, six foot seas! Mighty Whitey Rig was an inshore rig painted entirely white.

E-6275f088f2.text:
Okay, July 2nd, we head out on 78 degrees to Big Red. Beautiful day, running 3,000 RPM all day long. Not much luck at Big Red or Val’s Rig, but then we go to the Satellite Rig and Alex catches a 22-pound snapper, red snapper, that wins the junior and senior division of the Port Aransas Deep Sea Tournament.

We also caught 20 or so other snapper, two to six pounds. We trolled in with no takers except one amberjack. We caught and released several short of the legal limit. Forget what the limit was, digression there, but it was something like 35 or 40 inches, pretty good, pretty good size.

E-15669bb080.text: The Port Aransas Outboard Tournament, and Michael, Gary Einkauf and I fished. Beautiful seas all the way to Baker, but no hits.
E-15669bb080.note: They split up the tournament by engine spec, so the outboard tournament was our time to shine. Baker Reef was one of the coral reefs offshore. Baker, South Baker, Southern, and Hospital were all about 40 miles out. They catch marlin, sailfish, and wahoo out there.

E-243dafc8f0.text: Went North to the Way Ups then East to Satellite. 10 snappers, lots of chicken dolphin in weed lines. Other than that no luck trolling - beautiful calm day  10 gallons per hour.
E-243dafc8f0.note: The Way Ups were a cluster of rigs about 35 miles North of the jetty's that were in shallow water. A dolphin is another name for a mahi mahi. Chicken dolphin is just a little mahi mahi, usually 3-10 pounds.

E-06e80bdd06.text: Took Mike Hornsby and his friend, Herry, to Lone Pipe. Caught 6 Kings in about 20 minutes - came home in beautiful weather. Depth recorder out, also fuel pump between the auxilary and the main fuel line must have a constriction. Next week don't buy bait - we have 20 pounds of squid and ribbon fish in the freezer.
E-06e80bdd06.note: Lone Pipe was just a big ol' standpipe gas well sticking out of the water. Covered in barnacles, which attract fish.

E-d779898898.text: Guests were Dr Scott Holt and Dr Steve from the University of Texas Marine Science Center. We left at 6:30 am. Calm seas. Went to Scorpion, only one king, then to Val's Rig where the current was running so swiftly to the North that we could not tie on.
E-d779898898.note: They ended up naming Val's Rig after Val England where she caught those snapper there in one of the earlier trips.

E-be19a07009.text:
July 29, 1995, continued

We proceeded off shore about 1/2 mile where we found a great sargassom weed line. 
We stopped and chummed up six dolphin (3 to 10 lbs) and a 15 lb Wahoo. Dr. Holt's first Wahoo and Dr Steve's first Dolphin. We Ended the day at Big Red, catching and 27 Vermillion and red Snapper - Seas roughed up way home - N. wind 3-4 ft - Tropical Depression heading our way. Wahoo and Dolphin caught on ballyhoo under an octopus skirt
E-be19a07009.note: Vermillion are a type of snapper bright red as the name implies even brighter than red snapper, with some yellow along the gill plates. More importantly there wasn't a limit on them at the time, according to the Captain.

E-61f45f40e7.text: Charles and Judy Durban; after 2 days of waiting out Tropical Storm Gabrielle, we make it out on a heading 85° to 95 feet of water - lots of shrimp boats. Caught 6 kings real fast, no size though - all 12-20 lbs. Squally day - 4' to 5' seas, some rain. Again we used ballyhoo under seven strand octopus yellow and green. One great bait!
E-61f45f40e7.note:
Charles Durbin worked for the Business Men’s Assurance Company in Kansas City, and his wife Judy were really nice people. At the time, I was in the mortgage banking business for, gosh, a long time, 15 years, with Capital Mortgage Bankers, and Business Men’s Assurance Company was one of our main clients to purchase commercial mortgages that we generated in the Austin area. Worked with them a long time, and they loved to come down and fish every now and then.

Mentioned a few times before, ballyhoo are a great bait for mahi mahi and other fish. Small, about 10 inches long and with a big beak coming out from their lower jaw.

E-8f1abd29f1.text:
Chris Carothers, Mike Fleming, Nicole Beasley & me. Beautiful day! We leave at 7:00 - hit weed line at 80 degrees  off the bar in about 19 fathoms. Caught two nice dolphin. 10 -12 pounds. Weed line was patchy, and only about 300 yds, long. Seas running from the southeast to the north west. Then we go to Val's Rig past Big Red where we caught a limit of kings (12). A big shark (unseen but big by bite angle) cut three of our kings off right behind the gills! Fast action on kings, 2 on at at once a few times! Also caught 8 or so snapper, one at 6 lbs the largest.

I was the only witness. The shark was about as big as a suburban. It had at least 25 stripes. It probably was 325 pounds.
E-8f1abd29f1.note:
Captain Ed: On that trip, we finally—Michael was the only one on board that saw the shark. We tied onto the rig where we were snapper fishing and ran lines back where we were drifting ribbonfish for kings. We’d lost the two. We finally got a limit of kings in the boat, and then Michael kind of tugged on my shirt and said, “I saw him.” And I said, “You saw what?” And he said, “I saw the big shark.” And so that led to his entry here. 

I bet he weighed a lot more than that. I think he was one big tiger shark. They’re formidable beasts, and it was—after we caught a, you know, a gang of snapper on top of our limit of kingfish, I was glad to move away from there. There’s just a feeling around when you have a big predator like that right under your boat, who’s probably about, you know, at least 500 pounds. Time to move to another location in my book.

E-5a8d69156d.text: Dr. Scott Holt & Dr. Joan Holt on board with Mike and me. We ended up going north to the Way Ups. No kings taken. Not much sign of life until we tied on to a Way Up and caught a limit of nice snapper, released a 10 pound king. Beautiful day.

E-2e540d032d.text: Cameron Pratt, Lester Ducote, Mike Fleming, Alex Ducote, Will Cardwell and me head out to Big Blue. Pretty day but choppy with North wind. Not a strike at Blue! Starboard engine flooded out. Proceed to Port Aransas. Trolling along the way caught a Spanish mackerel. And then we tied on one rig, opposite of Perry Bass's house! Will at that rig caught 3 small ling, and Alex caught one huge one!! Headed in. Engine started when lifted to clean carburetor! Bad day.
E-2e540d032d.note: Mike was probably pissed he didn't get a ling cause he loved them so much. Perry Basset was a big millionaire and chairman of the UT mine science board. Did a ton of good environmentally down there, whatever Parks and Wildlife wanted he'd tried to fund. Engine trouble offshore always makes your stomach churn a little bit, says the Captain.

E-88c0444433.text: Lester Ducote and I start the morning at Baker. Anchored up on the main rock of North Baker. Limited on Kings in 10 minutes.Then trolled marlin lures to Dunnbar Reef. No strikes. About noon we went to the main oil platform in inside of Dunnbar- A7 in 33 fathoms. Limited on nice snapper. Three break offs on some really big (!!) bottom fish. Probably amberjack. Also saw some huge barracuda - 50 pounds plus. Caught a small 10 pounder that won his division of this weekend’s Corpus Christi Big Game Club tournament. At 2 o’clock we headed in looking for weed lines. Found one only about 500 yards long in 30 fathoms. We trolled ballyhoo under seven strand octopus, skirts, yellow and green and red and black. Three really nice bull dolphin 20 to 35 pounds and three smaller chicken dolphin. Agreat calm day all the way home at 30 to 32 mph. Used 10 gallons per hour.

E-83492c806c.text:
This entry should actually be dated September 16. 

Mike me and Gary Schmitt and wife Kathleen on board. North to Way Ups then to Satellite and then A7. Rough day, no fish (12 snapper!) To hell with going out when it’s so rough. 198 Fish so far this season (Sunday). 115 gallons - filled up and topped off with the oil - ready for next time. GPS started acting up as if power was shorting out. Long and lat would stay on, course over the ground and speed in miles per hour. The lower display consisting of true bearing and estimated time of arrival and distance to go would vanish, then the whole screen would go. I would push way point Port Aransas Jetty (this happened 55 miles out on the way in) then the whole screen would come back after about five minutes to re-require satellites. Very strange. We are checking the wiring today and if they’re ok we will send the unit back to Tulsa for fixing. Yesterday was really rough and it’s possible that something might have jarred loose.

Yesterday at A7 I baited the line with a live snapper on a single number eight hook - 120 pound wire on a 50 lb Penn and tossed it out to drift as we snapper fished. A big barracuda nailed him and I pushed the drag all the way up to stop him from getting under the rig. Stopped him and he made several short high speed runs slashing back and forth and the damned hook pulled out. I think a new state record ‘cuda lives there and I’m going to try him at every opportunity.
E-83492c806c.note: From the Captain: I remember that bastard. I dealt with him many days after that. God he was just there and he would lay out working his gills and look up at me.

E-34da3b6c76.text: First trip out since 9/16. Went to Big Red, Val, and A7 with Scott Holt - great day of weather but short of fish. 9 snapper.

E-cd1dda3a99.text: Rick Vaughn, Fred Dipple & me go to Big Red, and North. Rough - 1 king, 2 jacks, and 3 snapper.

E-9de191931a.text: Rough, 5-6 ft. Went South for 5 miles, we caught 2 jacks, Rick Vaughn fought & landed one in 45 min that was 25 lbs class.
E-9de191931a.note: Can't believe I went out in this shit, he says.

E-a6ebca7c9a.text:
Mike Gillespie, Mike Fleming and I leave the jetty at 9:00. At 90° MF decides it’s too rough (smart boy!) so we take him back to the dock. Mike G and I then go to the three standpipes 120° off bar. We catch 2 kings, one Atlantic sharp nose shark - and a large jack crevalle, about 30 lbs.

Swells 3-5' out of southwest. A norther arrives earlier than expected and a marine warning went out [over the radio] to return to port because of 60 knot winds, in a squall line just then hitting Rockport. We covered those 6 miles at 32 knot speed and hit the jetty just as it hit. Cold cold wind - saw a waterspout forming in the channel. Glad to be home.
E-a6ebca7c9a.note: Just a footnote, that really was a rough day, and there were tornadoes in the area from Portland, Rockport, Aransas Pass, all the way up to Port O’Connor. No damage, but it was beautiful to see.

E-51a6d90868.text:
Beautiful day with a cool north wind not 10-15 knots. Seas 3-5 ft from NE/SW. Went to same stand pipes as before, Mike is entered in the GCCA tournament, so we're looking for the big ones. No luck trolling today, so I rig a sea anchor off the bow that swings the Seahawk broadside to the swells, and I set up a chum line - this works!! We catch 3 kings and one shark in about 30 minutes with 3 other hard strikes breaking off. Crew is getting queasy so we return to port to drop Gillespie off. Mike F and I run up the channel to Pelican Island where we anchor looking for reds & trout. Mike catches one big 2 pound hard head.

The weigh in at at Woody's was fun! I string Mike's catch of the two kings, one shark, and a hardhead on a loop of line and he drags it to the weigh in booth. Every kid wins something, Mike won for biggest kingfish so he received a trophy and a really nice kingfish rod. We head to Bilmore's and purchase a 209 Penn Reel to celebrate his feat and complete his rig. A real fun day.

E-8baeaf29ad.text: Beautiful day. Mike (Fleming), me, Patrick (Fleming), and friend Josh went to Stand Pipes south of P.A. in 40 feet of water. We caught 1 king, one 39' ling trolling, then caught two more kings (drifting + chumming). Patrick and Josh were getting a little mal de mer, so we left for home. Mike caught his first King on his new kingfish rig - it really is smooth.
E-8baeaf29ad.note: Real close off Port A, real go to spot if the kings were in. Mal de mer is sickness of the sea, according to the captain

E-b06f4bea44.text: Mike G, Meredith and David (honeymooners) and me try to catch some kingfish. Pretty day, 10-15mph S.E. winds. Went to same standpipe as on 6/13, no luck, then West to Big Platform - we caught two kings (drifting and one trolling), lost 4 others that made long runs then broke free - very disappointing day.

E-dcead6d0b5.text: Dick Chote, Art Shepherd and Bryan (Dick's son in law) on board - Limit of kings, in close - run to Mighty Whitey for snapper - no keepers. Rough as hell!

E-1047d68004.text: Same crew - hooked a tarpon at the jetty! Fought him 3 hours and 45 min! Dick Chote did a fine job - broke the line as we were about to gaff him for pictures. Great Day!
E-1047d68004.note:
Just my memory of that day is that it was a spectacular hit. Kings were at the jetty. We were trolling at the center, heading out 90 degrees. When we hit him, he tail walked, did that beautiful jump that tarpon do with all the sound effects of their gills clattering, and he headed out to sea.

And by the time we had him up to the boat and we were trying to, when we say gaff him, I was trying to lip-gaff him to release him, he broke loose. But he was a beautiful fish. It was a great fight. And I don’t have any pictures, as I was busy. We’ll have to see if Dick or Art have any.

E-f8a3942aec.text: July 5 - Bill Hudspeth, Morgan Stone & me go to Southern — beautiful day + almost flat however fishing was slow. Caught one bonito at Southern on the way to the Jack Up Rig. Finally came in to the South Standpipes and caught 4 king’s.
E-f8a3942aec.note: Jack Up Rig was in a little oil field south of PA. It has all been wiped out by hurricanes since then. You could tell they were reworking Jack Up at the time because it had big cranes all over it.

E002.text: The first offshore trip was made in rough weather, 4-5 knot wind. NNE out to 16 fathoms looking for snapper. Cameron Pratt and Bill Hudspeth were with me. A dark rough day not conducive to fun fishing - we caught 2 snapper (too small) and a few triggers and called it a day.
E002.note:
Captain Ed: Bill Hudspeth and I stayed with Rick and Cameron Pratt at the lighthouse the night before, and Rick had to work, but Cameron accompanied Bill and I on this initial run.

A lot of these trips will use a direction and a depth as shorthand for navigation purposes. Captain Ed would maintain a heading on the compass from the jetty, where most of our trips began, follow it out to a certain depth. The sea floor out in the Gulf is a gradual slope so doing this would result in arriving at nearly the same spot with only the use of a compass and a depth finder.

E003.text: Patricia & Mike go with me on an impromptu snapper trip, beautiful weather - no fish.
E003.note: We didn’t go very far, as I recall. I think we went out about 10 miles just to show Patricia and Michael the boat and how it handled, and we had a good time just running around more than anything. Bought some shrimp from a shrimp boat out there and came home.

E-4eb0fe8c4f.text: Lester and I try to fish outside jetty for spanish mackerel - Rough seas! 5' and close together. 2 on, lost both.

E-e4f7ea18f5.text: First day of Deep Sea Roundup - Mike, Alex, Lester & me head first to Satellite and then to Apache. At Apache we trolled by and picked up a medium barracuda that won the Junior Division for Alex. Mike caught another barracuda 5-6 lbs and two rainbow runners. Real slow -- first time to use the squid family! It looked good but received no strikes.

E-bc61517692.text: Same crew, north to the Lone Pipe and then to Sparkyville. Caught four kings, released one, and broke off a few others. Could have put as many in the boat as we wanted to, but were looking for ling. Lost steering ability at Sparkyville, so we came back 27 miles on engines alone. Port engine forward, starboard engine in reverse in varying degrees. A real slow trip at six to seven knots.

E-a930e146cd.text: Fished with Bill Hudspeth and Bill Peace. Limit of kings, one mahi-mahi, pretty calm.

E-852874ad66.text: Hudspeth stayed in. Scott Holt on board. We got a limit of kings and one mahi-mahi. Caught all inside of ten fathoms. Went out 25 miles and no fish. Few fish, not worth the effort out there.

E-123f9864c8.text:
Fred Dippel, Rick Vaughn, Chris Drakenberg, engineers with the Cunningham Allen firm, and Scott Holt and I went to the jetties at 7 a.m. Calm seas, south-southeast, 10-mile-an-hour winds. Lots of kings at the pass. We caught six nice ones, 15 to 20 pounds, and saw several tarpon.

Decided to try offshore for mahi-mahi and wahoo. Found none at Hospital. Went to one rig southeast of Hospital and caught 11 snapper, 15 to 16 inches. Tomorrow we will stay inside and work on kings and Spanish, which we saw at the jetties.

E-f9c0e9589b.text: Seven nice Spanish mackerel in close on Hooties. Squall kept us in until 10 o’clock.

E-07d72c4323.text:
The Marbridge trip. I believe this is our 18th straight year to take these, take the Blue Water fishing team offshore. Beautiful days, calm seas, partly cloudy skies. I took Chris Winslow, Carl French, and Brian Ring on my boat, and Jim Harmon took six men, including Bob Fulbright, on the Barracuda.

We went to Southern, and both boats took limits of kings over the rocks drifting ribbonfish. Our eight kings included one in the 25- to 28-pound class, another smaller dolphin, and a nice four-pound snapper. We then went 328 degrees off the Southern Rig, 5.5 miles to a wreck. The Barracuda picked up four big amberjack, but then Jim’s LORAN went out, and we could not find the wreck again.

We then went inshore about six miles where we found an anchored shrimper, and we chummed up a few blackfin tuna. Chris caught a nice one of some 22 to 25 pounds, and that was it. All told, we boated 350 pounds of fish, which ought to feed the ranch for a few days. Good, good times with old friends.

E-5c2b8e7793.text: Chuck, Virginia, Patrick and I go to the North Jetty to troll for kings and tarpon. No takers. We then went out to some shrimp boats anchored up six and a half miles out, 125 degrees off the bar. Caught one nice Spanish mackerel and one other strike. Pretty choppy, but a nice day. Came in to be at Mr. Robinson’s house for the 11 a.m. kickoff between Notre Dame and UT. Tonight is Mr. George Robinson’s 90th birthday party! Good duck hunting today.

E-00d722132c.text: Used the Seahawk, which was a very comfortable duck boat. Hunted Lighthouse Shore and St. Jo shoreline. Limit of ducks, half a limit in the morning and half a limit in the afternoon.

E-fe33d59514.text: First trip offshore this year. Bill Hudspeth and I go to the Southern Rig via rig number 831. Eight snapper. Fantastic sargassum weed line inshore, half a mile off of Southern. Trolled for a while and strangely no fish.

E-a16ea80c35.text: Joe Blankenship, Mike and I just had to try for kings just off the jetty. A little early for that. No luck. Worked all day long on the teak trim. Boat is running well and soon will be shined up and ready for the season.

E-ddfd059bac.text: Mike and I fished with Ben Vaughn, his son James, John Treadwell, and Chad Ohlendorf. Beautiful day, but we overran the kings. We started at a shrimper anchored 90 degrees off the bar, five miles out, and got one strike. Then to Scorpion Rig, 17 miles further out, and only caught two blue runners. We then ran northwest to Little Rigs and no luck again. Little early.

E-11cf3f8630.text:
Mike, Chad Olandorf, and I go out and fish for kings between the Bell Buoy and the three standpipes, six miles southeast of Port Aransas. Chad catches a 27-pound king and Mike a large blacktip shark after a 20-minute fight. I gaffed him in the tail and had him port side with the tail as high as my head and the shark’s pectoral fin still in the water!

I should have shot him, but instead was going to tail-rope him and tow him for a while. After about three minutes of this indignity, the shark came to, ripped the gaff hook out of his tail, and took off with the wrap around the gaff handle. The gaff (it floats) gave him the resistance he needed to break the line. Mike and I are both sick with disappointment. I consider him a caught fish, as he was wired and incapable for such a long time. However, Mike does not see it that way. I believe him to be approximately seven feet long and probably 85 to 100 pounds.

Mike recovered well and caught a 20-pound blacktip shark 20 minutes later. The boys caught two more 15-pound-class kings, and then we came in. All fish were caught drifting with the sea anchor out on the starboard side of the bow. We chummed to attract the rascals.

E-1680b03a4c.text: Mike and I fished with Rick and Cameron and Chad Ohlendorf, same area as noted before. Fish were scattered, but we found quite a variety. Drifted and chummed for an hour with no results. Then we started trolling with ribbonfish below small egg sinkers and did quite well. Chad caught a big 27-pound jack crevalle, and Cameron caught her first ling, which was the main prize today. We also caught five nice kings in the 10 to 15 pound range, a Spanish mackerel, and Mike caught a 10-pound bonita.

E-798bd64a09.text:
Mike and I fished with Will Houston and sons David and Bradley, and Chad Ohlendorf. Pretty choppy, but we were entered in the GCCA’s Take a Kid Fishing tournament, so we decided to give it a go. No strikes in close, so we fished the ships in the Farewell Anchorage area, out about five and a half miles. The kings were there!

It was great to see my godson David catch his first kingfish. Each boy caught one, with Bradley’s being the largest. Mike’s was the largest king caught by an eight-year-old boy. All kids won a nice trophy and a spinning rod and reel.

E-e2a233e670.text: Mike and I fished with Walter and Will Cardwell on a brief afternoon trip. Will catches one Atlantic sharpnose shark, but he gets a little queasy, so we head in. Total time one hour, but a good time with nice folks.

E-a0b22e406e.text:
Our office bunch, with the exception of Nick von Kreisler, who had family business to attend to, came to our house for a bay and offshore trip. Susan Haney, Bob Swanson, and Lester Ducote fished with me, and John Avery and Tom Curtis fished with Gary Einkauf. They are fly fishing.

Southeast winds, 15 mile an hour steady, made it rough, but the sun was shining bright and it wasn’t too bad. We caught our limit of eight kings between the jetty and the southeast standpipes. None real big. They were all in the range of 10 to 14 pounds. Two were caught on the black and white squid skirt with ballyhoo. I think this lure will be a great performer later in the year on wahoo.

Equipment problems caused us to come in slow. Seems I’ve got a bad ring in the port engine, which will be fixed next week. Also this afternoon replaced a head gasket on the starboard engine. GPS was giving some erratic readings, so after talking to the Lowrance factory, the unit and module was going by UPS to Tulsa for a fix-up. While out of the water, the hull will be compounded and waxed with a new copper bottom painted on.

Seahawk will be ready for some serious fishing when we get back from California. We’re going out there to meet Chris Carothers on his return from Australia and to take Michael to Disneyland. Good summer so far.

P-page-029-prefix.text: Well, there’s more to that. Great party at the house last night. Rick and Cameron joined our office bunch for a crab boil, grilled some kings and two redfish fillets, which were the total catch of John and Tom. Lots of fun. Broke up about 12:30.

E-9e4df49806.text: Too rough for offshore or bay! Southeast winds 20–25. Canceled bay trip with Smokey and slept in. Terry Bray and Jim Garrison arrived at 6 p.m. Good dinner at Pelican’s.

E-93337a86e0.text:
Terry Bray, Jim Garrison and I head south to the old Exxon platform and catch one decent 20-pound king. Terry gets feeling a little queasy, so he elects to be let out on a vacant oil well for an hour nap while Jim and I try to stir up some kings. No luck, so we pick up Terry and run offshore to standpipes where we catch another four small kings. Great to be with these old friends again.

Despite port engine’s ring problem, it ran well. Both engines humming at 4,000 RPM. Nice seas, bright day. After naps, we will grill some king steaks and shrimp tonight!
E-93337a86e0.note: Stand Pipes is an area of small gas wells southeast of Port Aransas. Captain Ed notes that he let Terry off on the old Exxon platform. He showed great athletic ability in jumping from the bow up to the ladder, which was a distance about five feet, and he did the same athletic endeavor successfully getting back in the boat after his nap.

E-2937dc666b.text:
Chris, Mike, Reed Fleming and I come down for the glorious Fourth of July. Great weather, great fireworks, great dinner, wahoo steaks and grilled shrimp, with our guests Rick and Bonnie Vaughn. However, the port engine on the Seahawk, which has suffered a stuck ring, blown bearing, etc., was not ready to go fishing. I left the key to the skiff in the boat barn in Austin. So due to the great weather, we limped out on the reliable starboard engine.

Great day, light south winds at five miles an hour, blue-green water a few miles out. We went to the third set of wells due south of the jetty, probably in 45 feet of water. Only one small amberjack landed until Chris caught a super good king, 40-pound class, on a drifted ribbonfish while tied onto an oil platform.

We have misplaced the measurements, but he appeared to be a twin of Mike’s big king caught May 20th of 1995, that had a girth of 24 inches and a length of 54 inches from nose to the fork of the tail. A real beauty.

The fish was found to have recently given a snapper fisherman a thrill of a lifetime, as we found a number six Mustad long-shank hook attached to what appeared to be a four-inch section of 100-pound-test monofilament deep in his stomach. He gave Chris a great fight despite this possibly uncomfortable item in his stomach.

E-cad8ce18ef.text:
Tournament crew consisted of me, Mike and Chris, Alex and Lester. Too heavy seas running, we decide, for the kids, so Chris and Lester and I go. First day of the Deep Sea Roundup, heavy seas running southeast, fair skies. We went first to Big Red and then to Satellite, and never found the fish.

We ended up at Yellowlegs, which is rig number 672-A, 27 degrees 58 minutes 65 seconds by 96 degrees 17 minutes 48 seconds, where we caught several blue runners for bait and put them down onto a steel Monel leader.

We broke off two big amberjacks and one kingfish before I rigged the 400-pound braided leader and tightened the drag to zero and caught a 22-pound amberjack that bent the rod and me to the breaking point. I led briefly in the tournament for that division and ended up in third place.

We also used a Monel wire and a 50-pound Penn, and I know it will work well on wahoo. We caught three kings. It’s fun and there’s no drag, so you get to feel the real power of the fish. Three amberjack hits with one in the boat.

E-3c94fd88c1.text:
A very frustrating day. More tomorrow.

Mike, Chris, Alex, Lester and I never have seen such a disappointing day. We lost some large fish, one broken line, and two unexplained de-hookings. We went north 30 miles, then out to Big Red and ended up at Yellowlegs, but two boats there, so we went three miles north to a rig that looked good.

We caught some live bait there and rigged them to the steel leader rig and made others using the Penn 50s with 10-foot shark leaders. Alex hooked an almost minimum-length amberjack, 30 inches, nose to fork, that we had to release.

The real heartbreaker was Mike’s ling. With just 15 minutes left in the tournament, I rigged a live blue runner on a 50-pound Penn with a float and let it drift off behind the boat. A really good ling, 40 inches, 35-pound class, gave Mike a great fight for five minutes before the fish just let go of the blue runner. Apparently he was never really hooked, which is amazing considering the bend in the heavy rod. And what a fitting end to a disappointing tournament for us.

E-ed2b609889.text:
Bill Hudspeth with me on a trip to Southern. Light to medium seas, two- to three-foot, southeast wind. Water temperature of 86 degrees. We made the 45-minute run in just about two hours, just under two hours, looking for wahoo, but kingfish were all over the rock. We caught our limit of four in about 10 minutes. The Huntington drone spoons picked up two, and the black and red octopus skirts over the ballyhoo put another two in the boat.

The real excitement was in trying to make a routine hookup on the oil rig located at the south end of Southern Reef. Without a doubt, this was the most frightening moment in my 30 years of offshore fishing. I eased up to the rig from the down-current side and Bill hooked the shepherd’s crook over a rig stairway. This was our usual method of operation.

I then put both engines in reverse, and the boat, instead of going backwards, leaped forward, ramming the rig at the northeast corner, tearing off my bow rail and badly scraping the gel coat off of the port bow in two places. The impact threw Bill down, and for a few seconds I thought he was really hurt. It seems that the motor steering cable on the starboard engine was not correctly installed, which caused the engines to stay in forward gear, and it accelerated with the gear lever in reverse. John Price said he would take care of the problem at no cost.

E-1bc054bfa7.text:
After this adventure, we had a fairly good time with the starboard engine off. As Bill said, “Kill it before it kills us.” We tied onto the rig as planned and caught four nice rainbow runners. Then went trolling and picked up a small mahi-mahi. No weed anywhere.

We went to the Leaner Rig, number 781, 25.5 miles out, and on the first pass Bill caught a really nice 15-pound barracuda on a blue-green squid skirt. Beautiful run home at 30 miles an hour with a following sea.

We cleaned the fish at the lighthouse pier and had a great dinner with Rick and Cameron, Cactus Pryor and his family. After they left, Cameron, Rick, Bill and I had a few drinks on the porch while watching Rick, who plays a very, very good guitar, sing about every Willie Nelson, Hank Williams, and Hank Snow song that was ever made. God, it was a very fine time. Great friends.

Occasionally a coyote would howl back at us from across the Lydia Ann Channel from St. Joe Island. After a good night’s sleep, we motored back from the lighthouse to our slip and then headed back to Austin.

E-5f1bfaa81c.text: Chris, Michael and I leave after a Park 22 meeting to Port Aransas. We fish, or try to, August 8th. Beautiful day, but lots of southeast wind. Went to the standpipes and headed back in. One strike, no fish. Went to the lighthouse where Mike caught some great stone crabs for his aquarium. Fun time.

E-216d81944a.text:
The first day of our annual Marbridge trip. Jim Harmon on the Barracuda took Bob Fulbright and five men. I took Chris Winslow, Rob, and Jerry. Beautiful day with light southeast chop. We ran to Eastern Rock (north approximately three and a half miles from Hospital), where the bottom rises from 240 feet to 180 feet.

The rock had lots of kings. We caught eight nice ones in one hour. We also took three small sharks and one amberjack. Jim’s boat didn’t do as well, with only three kings and approximately five nice snapper, plus Doug caught a nice blackfin tuna.

On the way out, I registered a good-looking well for snapper. I labeled it Black 784 in the GPS. It is about seven miles inside of Eastern. Also on the way back, I went a bit south to check out a well I called Cuda. There were rainbow runners all over it and one big barracuda there. But we were homeward bound at 33 miles out, and I was bone tired.

We all had a great time. The guys enjoyed coming to the house and looking at their pictures on the wall from 15 years ago. I logged in two Eastern GPS sites today. The first is the center of the reef, and the second one was the plateau where sonar showed a large group of snapper.

E-279fce04a9.text:
Scott and Joan Holt accompanied me on a great trip offshore to Eastern Rock (actually part of Hospital Reef). We drifted baits and chummed up five nice kings in the 12 to 20-pound class. We had several fish hit and break off, probably as many as we caught. I caught a nice 12-pound red snapper on the bottom, but by noon the bite was over.

We then proceeded 13 miles southwest to Rick Darling’s well, which is a submerged, capped-off old well. It’s real small and difficult to locate in 180 feet of water, and although I found it twice, our buoy did not hold well. Still, we caught 10 nice three- to 10-pound snapper. Scott also caught a 37-inch ling of some 15 pounds that fought on top as usual, and it was very exciting.

As we were collecting our buoy, a small group of mahi-mahi were under it, as they often are. We proceeded to catch 18 of them, all in the two- to four-pound range, but tasty eating size.

Beautiful day with some southeast chop on the way out, max speed 17 knots. Coming back in with the gentle sea, we were hitting 27 to 30 knots all the way in. That night we had a super party given by Dr. Sweppy for fellow University of Texas Marine Science Center advisory members. Great time.

E-248c86f2bc.text:
Son Michael and Scott Holt aboard. Real windy day. Tried for Spanish. No luck. Called it a day after 9:30 a.m. Scott has the longitude and latitude on a submerged well about 35 miles out that we will try next time.

Had a good conversation with Scott about the feasibility of us starting a snook restocking program for the Texas coast via the talent of the University of Texas Marine Science Board.

E-c306261842.text: Beautiful day. Light southwest winds at five miles an hour. Me and Mike tried the jetties. Had one strike on a ballyhoo, then nothing, so we went to Lydia Ann, and there we caught two legal Spanish mackerel, and Mike caught three skipjack on free shrimp. One was a 22-inch dandy.

E-6207522af4.text: Patricia and I fished together offshore for the first time in probably 10 years. We had a great time. Left the dock at 9:30 and docked again at 12. We caught two small kings, 10 pounds or so, along the south standpipes. Enough for a good dinner that night with Rick and Cameron. Beautiful day, almost calm, with low humidity and a clear post-norther sky. Lots of fun.

E-87785c013c.text: Scott Holt and I and John and Large John Oliver, in their new 25-foot Boston Whaler, tried to go to Southern. Rough as a cob. We turned back short at the south standpipes. North wind, five- to eight-foot seas. Home by 9 a.m.

E-4bcfa4937e.text: Scott and Joan Holt go with me for another try. We tried Southern, but it was too rough, so we stopped at the 25-mile rig, 124 degrees off the bar, and caught 10 nice snapper and three triggerfish. And the first snapper was cut in two by a barracuda.

E-7bb3604ad0.text:
Patricia Ann surprises me with a fantastic birthday gift, twin Johnson 175-horsepower Evinrude engines for the Seahawk. They’re supposed to be the best engines made at this time for fuel efficiency. I’m delighted.

They will be installed by Island Boatworks. John Price hopes to have them by June 1st on the boat. While this work is being done, we will also be installing a new, higher and stronger bow rail and repainting the deck and painting on a new bottom, blue this time, on my trusty boat.

E-57090c5aeb.text: First time through the jetties with the new engines. Guests were Todd Hanna and Marianne Ferguson. Engines ran great, very quiet. Rough, dark weather helped out with lots of smoke from Mexico. Went only to Little Rigs, no hits, and came home.

E-a97561328b.text: Same foul weather, Todd only on this trip. He caught a nice 20-pound jack crevalle at the standpipes, 150 degrees. Ten fathoms. Sun shining, but the smoke haze is still very thick and limited our visibility to a quarter of a mile to a half a mile. Came home quick.

E-fa3fcb2866.text:
Todd Rubel and Joe Sullivan flew into the Corpus Christi Airport. I picked them up and took them to our house. We had a good visit. They were my partners on the Park 22 building project.

However, June 13th, clear skies but rough, rough seas, four- to six-footers, southeast winds 20 miles an hour. We never had a strike. The wind seems to be relentless. It has been blowing steady, as it seems, for a month. Natives are starting to get crazier than usual around here.

E-c550df3542.text:
First day of the Port Aransas Deep Sea Roundup. My crew is Bill Hudspeth, Lester Ducote, Albert Rathmill, all seasoned hands. John Oliver’s boat, the Double O, will stay with us since they are just starting to fish offshore in their new 25-foot Whaler. John’s crew includes William Page and Clint Small.

We run to the Black 784 rig and put in baits there as we start trolling to Eastern. We have no hits until we reach the reef, and then we have a triple knockdown on kingfish and put all on the boat.

About this time, John Oliver calls to say that they have a big fish on. Calls between us over the next 30 minutes convince me that the boys are on to truly a big one. Bets are in our boat for yellowfin tuna, shark, etc. John reports after an hour that they’ve got a glimpse of him. He’s at least 60 pounds and is a blackfin tuna. Since the Texas record is about 35 pounds, I tell them to play him easy, get him in the boat, and head for the dock, as a new state record is at hand.

E-a355f8a7f0.text:
All this time, we are in sight of each other, so we head over to the fight to offer what passes as expert guidance. On the way, we start seeing lots of flying fish, some bunches of a dozen or more. Since this is a sure sign of dorado, I add two large ribbonfish under skirts with no weights on both outriggers, and put the Yo-Zuri nonita and a big Huntington spoon on a steel line on flatlines.

After making a pass around Double O to see their tuna, which turned out to be 26 pounds, and secured Clint Small a second-place trophy in the tournament. Tuna always fight like ten men. We had a knockdown on the port outrigger, and Hudspeth got into the chair and commenced reeling. He said the fish didn’t feel like much. Just then the Penn 50 reel started screaming and ripping off line, and to the port a fine sailfish took to the air.

He made three spectacular jumps. He came to the boat after about a 15-minute fight, and I wired him and Lester Ducote gaffed him. He was 70 inches long and weighed 57 pounds. He was Bill’s first sailfish, and it was also the first sailfish on the Seahawk. And it was just time to hang one up.

Bill was interviewed at the dock on Channel 6, and lots of photos taken. He was in first place for a while until displaced by a 75-pounder and a 67-pounder. I think that we finished third in sailfish division.

A really fun day, but the seas were rough as usual, four to six-footers, and damn, I’m ready for it to calm down. The boat is really taking a pounding on these days. My forward cross brace on the T-top broke. It broke its weld in the starboard cabinet of the console, busted loose. I need a day to get everything back together.

We have a good party, feasting with the Double O crew’s tuna as the main course. Great time.

E-67243d16d9.text:
Rick Vaughn, Albert Rathmell and me, and John Oliver’s Double O and his crew head north 50 degrees and run 25.5 miles to a cluster of gas wells looking for kings, ling and crevalle. Since the seas are four to six feet at least we won’t take the pounding like we took them yesterday, taking them on the bow. Also, leaders in the above categories are small, and we should have a good chance of catching up.

Our boat gets into the kingfish, catching 15 and releasing all but five for the table. All of ours in the 12 to 25-pound range. The last two were our largest, but then the bite was over and we could not find a 31-pounder, which was the number to beat. Double O boats one fish. 

We tied up to a gas well which is now waypoint 42 on my GPS. Dog tired after a shrimp dinner at the tournament headquarters, I get a good 12 hours’ sleep.

E-ec72938425.text: Scott Holt, Cameron and I do Southern. No luck. Squally. Ran a good race and won with a storm.

E-8e84d518c3.text: Another water haul. Rough and no luck.

E-f2316f11d0.text: Son Michael and I take the skiff to Lighthouse Creek and catch a dozen nice big blue crabs. Too tough for offshore this weekend.

E-7cb3734825.text:
Scott Holt, Mike Fleming, Chad Ohlendorf and I cross the bar at 7:15 a.m. on a course of 80 degrees for Big Red and friends. Slow snapper fishing with lots of 14-inchers caught and released. Fifteen inches was the minimum limit.

We then went to rig number 45, MU-A85, in 45 fathoms, and we found some nice snapper. 16 to 18 inches, and Mike caught a big 60-pound grouper. We ended up with 18 snapper, six vermilion snapper, one grouper, three triggerfish, and five or six blue runners (Scott Holt’s cat food).

Seas were almost calm. Left the jetty at 34 miles per hour and did not touch the throttle for an hour. Beautiful day! Burned 68 gallons over a 10-hour trip, 6.8 gallons per hour. This compares well with the 10 gallons per hour rate of the old engines, 30% savings on gas. Oil use is difficult to calibrate, but the new engines burn much less, maybe a 60% savings in oil.
E-7cb3734825.note: Hearing about that grouper brings back a really vivid memory for me as a kid. The weight of this massive creature I'm pulling up from the depths, gradually getting to so I can see him more clearly close to the surface.

E-49cff0443e.text: Guests on board are Robert Rivers, Will Houston, David and Bradley Houston, and son Mike. John Oliver’s boat with Steve and Becky Rivers runs alongside of us. Lousy rough day. Northeast winds at 15–25 miles per hour. Norther has been blowing for two days and nights. We went to the Little Rigs north and then to Scorpion. No hits. Boat running great in six- to seven-foot seas. Glad to be home.

E-e53db0dfd3.text: Doug Seymour and Brad on board. We hook a nice striped marlin on a stinger jet head down the middle between the harbor and the VV Buoy. About 10 o’clock, we hook up a bigger striper, but he comes off after I was in the chair five minutes. This one was on the flying fish jet head by Captain Doug Hague, (which is a custom-built lure over there). Things are picking up. Hit the second one off Keauhou on the way to Red Hill.

E-b9ab6b7191.text:
Doug Seymour, son Michael, and Doug’s son Daniel on board. One mile, 270 degrees west of the harbor, we get a strike on the stinger. Doesn’t stick. Then the port rigger goes off. Again, no fish. All the time moving at nine knots. Then the starboard long rigger, and this time he’s on for a minute or two, then off. We all think it was a chucker, or a shortbill spearfish. Pretty slow.

We finally hook a good ono off of Pine Tree and lose him at the gaff. Damn depressing. Ono liked the black and white heavy jet head, and the chucker hit the Yo-Zuri rig, Old Faithful, Doug Hague’s lure that looks like a flying fish, and the stinger was on the Kona-made Geoff Head.

Today we saw a mature humpback whale completely clear the water on a magnificent leap. A whale-watching boat was cheering him on about 200 yards south of us as we fished around Otek Point.
E-b9ab6b7191.note: Captain Ed: I mean, everything cleared the water. You could see his sulfur-yellow belly and the pleats in his stomach skin. Very formidable. We were about 300 yards away, which was close enough.

E-434ca2e111.text:
Great day. Hit an otado of about 15 pounds on the corner of the grounds. Mike catches him on the 50-pound Penn. We work south with no luck on the high road to the Kitchen. But when we retrace our route, we have a double hookup at Waypoint 21. Michael catches, tags, and releases a black marlin of all things, of about 100 pounds. Fixed pectoral fins. Beautiful fish. First black marlin I’ve ever seen, or any of us have ever seen.

The route to use is the harbor to number 21, then north, lining up the lighthouse with Titty Butt to the 300-fathom shelf, and then west to fish the ledge of the grounds. Then back the same way at 21, turn toward the Kona Hilton, and run into the shelf at 300 fathoms. Follow to the Kitchen and back.

Also use the church run, whereby we line up the Catholic church steeple with the Moroni statue on top of the Mormon temple, and run into the shelf and back out. This is going to be a great year. Doug Hague’s lures are great. The flying fish, root beer colored, are getting all the hits.
E-434ca2e111.note: An "otado" (frequently spelled otaru) is a local Hawaiian term for a large skipjack tuna or aku that weighs over 20 pounds (typically 16 to 30 pounds).

E-6d9a237ee7.text: Jim Rizzuto and Doug on board. No luck all day. Squally and spitting rains at times. Got close to two pygmy sperm whales for photos off Keauhou.
E-6d9a237ee7.note: Jim Rizzuto was Phil Rizzuto’s cousin, famous New York Yankee shortstop. Jim is a sports writer for the newspaper out there on the Big Island.

E-83ffaf111a.text: Patricia and Joanne Mickelson on board, whale watching and fishing. Heavy on the whale watching by the airport. Some big humpbacks got closer than intended. Should have some great pictures.
E-83ffaf111a.note:
Dad dates this as February 29th which would have been a Leap Day but there wasn't one in 2001. 

Captain Ed: An aside on that, that was one day that was really crazy. Those big humpbacks, we were getting close to them, maybe 150 yards away, and they both went down under the water, a little bit of an angle toward us, which bothered me some. But looked down and, God, these things bigger than school buses, both of them went under our boat, I would say probably 20 feet down in that beautiful clear water. I’ll never forget that sight. Thank God they came up about 100 yards starboard side of us and didn’t kill us all.

E-7179b3bc00.text:
Great trip. Earl Regador and I tag and release a nice 50-pound chucker at the south end of the grounds. Then 15 weke ʻulas. Then a 22-pound ahi, a yellowfin tuna, and another one at The Pines at 20 fathoms. Great trip.

Chucker was caught on Doug Hague’s flying fish run out through the long port rigger, ahi on the blue and pink ono jet head.
E-7179b3bc00.note: I had to look weke ʻula up, it's a beautiful little red goatfish that lives in the reefs. Evidently some can contain toxins that cause vivid hallucinations and nightmares if eaten.

E-99faeb8fb1.text: Doug Seymour and I head for the grounds. Nothing would stick today. Two ono hits and a big marlin hit everything we had out. Briefly on with the big Yo-Zuri. Frustrating. The grounds again are hot. Some bait showing up. Nine billfish so far on the boat.

E-8828e9c0cb.text: Doug and I screwed again. Not one strike down south.

E-f5b6f8677c.text: Marius and George, both South Africans working for Guy Cellier  went with me today. Winds north at 20 knots, four- to six-foot seas. Only one hit, but it stuck. A nice 25-pound mahi-mahi on the faithful Yo-Zuri.
E-f5b6f8677c.note: Captain Ed: I remember those fellas, and Guy Cellier, I don’t remember his name and what he looked like. I can’t remember what he did or why he was fishing with us.

E-cd9858ec9e.text: Doug and Bomboy on board. Went south off Red Hill, had a hit on the Yo-Zuri jet head. Old Faithful got off. Rough day. Squally northwest wind.
E-cd9858ec9e.note: Captain Ed: Bomboy was a guide there in the harbor, a rather colorful 120 percent Hawaiian. Remember, he ran a boat directly across from where we tied up.

E-f456a8e0c5.text: John Bagwell and Mike on board, no strikes.

E-5392492051.text: Doug, son Michael, and his friend Ivan on board. We find a beautiful rip four miles out and near the thousand-fathom line, running north and south, lots of bait showing. We catch a 26-pound mahi-mahi and another hard strike. Work the Pine Shore and have one strike from an ono, and head in. Needed to get back to Waimea at 3 o’clock. Pretty day.

E-502d774e29.text: Guy Cellier, children Peter and Laura, and Marvin on board. No strikes. Pretty weather, no birds, no bait.

E-14b214405d.text:
Doug and I head out to the F buoy, get a spearfish, a chucker, in the baits. Two knockdowns, couldn’t hook him. Then to the south porpoise school off of Red Hill. One tap on the stinger, then a great hit on the port outrigger, on for a minute and then gone, probably ahi.

At 3:30, the sound of a reel is heard, but only for 20 seconds or so. We look around, and the 130s, the 130 Penns and the 80 are in fine shape with no slippage of rubber bands. Then we notice that the 150 on top of the T-top rack, in the stinger position, is bent double and line is running out damn near to the end of the spool. The strike was so hard that the clicker was disabled. With 700 yards of line out, it broke at the knot. Very disappointing and very unprofessional of us.

Good news is that the lure with the new Mylar wings got five hits today, and it’ll pay off soon. Hits were on the Yo-Zuri as usual, and the lost lure was a small Yo-Zuri jet, pink and blue with nylon wings that made it look like a flying fish.

E-8840da11ac.text:
4/21  Mike and his friend Mike Guevara & I took both to "C's". Soupy Dave began trolling two yozuris on the rigger. I & Capt. Hoag on the other hand one ballyhoo under a pink blue skirt. Cuda & nice mahi bull 26# 28#. Another followed then in but I went to busy to bring him in double, then just approaching Ul Soupy he hit a bull on strip. Guevara got the leader, neat bull - 22# I was below. Mike (Soupy) had a bigger fish on the 50# Penn, make two above the hook - lost fish on the yozuri. Great day!

Son Michael and his friend Mike Gouveia and I head south to C buoy and begin trolling the two Yo-Zuris on the riggers. A Captain Hague on the stinger and a ballyhoo under a pink and blue skirt catch a nice mahi double, a 26-pounder and a 28-pounder. Another followed them in, but I was too busy to throw him a ballyhoo.

Then we went south approaching the UU buoy. We hit a double on striped marlin. Gouveia got into the leader. It was a 25-pound, very small marlin, so we released it. Mike had a bigger fish on the 50-pound Penn, and he threw the hook. Both fish were on the Yo-Zuris. Great day.

E-08d7f4aefe.text: Doug Seymour and I went straight out 260 degrees for seven miles before stopping to troll. Picked up a nice ono, 30 pounds, on the ballyhoo under a red and black skirt. One other hit before that one stuck. That was it for the day. Most of the fleet went south. It’s the 66th trip for the Seahawk out of Kona.

E-19634be066.text: Bill Hudspeth, Jim Garrison and I go to GPS rig number 56 north. Details later. Six kings, nothing showing at anchored ships. Rough seas, six to eight. Orange and black Exterminator was the bait of choice. Kings hitting them extremely hard. Many hits, about 80% hookups. Size of kings were fair. Two were in the 20-pound class and the other four were 15-pounders. Cameron and Rick join us for fish steaks that night on the grill.

E-page-043-june-06.text:
With wind still howling 20 to 30 knots, we set crab traps along the lighthouse shore. We caught 60 big blue crabs, mostly males. Another good party. Steve Cochran from Houston, who was my old UT roommate, joins us for an unproductive trout trip but a great crab boil.

One of these days the damn wind will quit. The fish are out there. We just need some decent seas to run in. June 5th, the water was a gorgeous color, deep blue/green color change, but so rough that some of the fun of being out there was diminished.

E-e593a8be00.text:
Chris Carothers, Bill Hudspeth, Albert Rathmill and me are the first-day team, with Hill Morrison filling in, fishing with us on the second day.

Day one, we found a color change five miles out inside of Southern. Lots of hits. One small ling and a few small chicken dolphin in the color change. We went to a well south of Southern and caught two nice barracuda. One that Hudspeth caught was in the 20-pound range at the end of the first day.

Day two, stormy seas, went to a little well southeast and decided to turn back. 

Seahawk will be coming to Kona, Big Island of Hawaii, the first part of ’99.

E-46c2b0b713.text: Seahawk will be loaning to Kona the first part of Oct 55!! It arrived at the Kawaihae Harbor on Friday, October 19th. We pick it up and haul it to the Kona Honokōhau Harbor, and at 4 p.m. Monday, November 22nd, Earl blesses the boat and gives it its Hawaiian name, [Eokai?], which is the translation for Seahawk. Bob and Carlene Jenkins are with Patricia, Mike, and I for the occasion.

E-8fdb13547b.text:
Tom Siebert helps rig the outriggers and cable. Lost on the 100's and one 80's as we went thru the harbor

Tom Seibert?, who was a local charter captain, helped me rig the outriggers and double lines on the 130s and 180-pound Penn.
E-8fdb13547b.note: Tom was a local charter captain. Continued on the next page.

P-page-045-prefix.text:
We went through the harbor at 10:20 and headed south. Not a strike all day. Port engine picked up some water and was running a bit rough. We fished all day and returned to the ramp at 4 o’clock. Saw a small pod of minke whales. Real calm but unusually hazy.

Changed filters, and the mechanic was supposed to change the engine filters on Wednesday. We were entered in the Kona Turkey Day tournament on Saturday.

E-26ddaedba6.text:
Son Michael Fleming, Rick Pratt, and Tom Seibert and I register as team number 12 for the Kona Turkey Bowl. We have a shotgun start of 37 boats, all leaving at 7 a.m. from the Green Buoy. We run south and fish offshore of Red Hill to Captain Cook. We caught two mahi, nice ones, one of 29 pounds and another of 28. A great double.

I made a dumb mistake of gaffing the second one and putting him in the forward fish box. I slipped, and the enclosed hook went through my skin and out about an inch and a half later. Came out again in my left leg. Didn’t hurt, but looked like hell. No bolt cutters on board, so we just taped it down with duct tape. And it was not very comfortable, but it wasn’t very uncomfortable either.

E-476f1f444a.text: After the weigh-in, we came in third on mahi-mahi. I was taken by Patricia to EMS, where they removed the hook. So all is well. I’ll be more careful next time. It was great to come in at 32 knots, mahi-mahi flags flying. Beautiful day.
E-476f1f444a.note: Continued from the previous page. This should be displayed with page 46 but it's on page 45.

E-31bdd85bbf.text: Earl Regador and his brother Moki go with me south to Captain Cook. No luck. We had two mahi-mahi on briefly at the VW buoy. Nice day.

E-6f9e517116.text:
First day out this year. John Bagwell and I troll from the Green Buoy to the grounds. Lots of bait. We lose a nice mahi-mahi on live bait, then catch a 30-pounder. Hooties out again. We catch a couple of nice otado which are middle-aged aku, and another aku. Both rigged live.

We see an immense tail come behind the baits. I thought it was a huge marlin. The Penn 130 portside line goes down, reel screaming. Ends up at 155 pounds after being gutted and gilled, so probably 175. Thresher shark. Fun day.

E-4c75798634.text: Earl and I and son Mike. No strikes, no bait, no birds.

E-344131c3bd.text: Tom Siebler and I head south at dawn. Between VW and Red Hill, we get a good 45-pound spearfish on the long port rigger on Penn 80, my first official one. No other strikes. He was off of Red Hill.

E-3026d682c7.text: John Bagwell, son Mike, Alex Michelson and I fish all day with no strikes. See several humpback whales and a pod of pilots, but no fish. Slow time of the year, they say.

E-19c3775cf3.text: Todd Rubel and I. We go to VW, C Buoy. No strikes, no birds, nothing. Five trips since New Year’s. One thresher, one mahi, one spearfish, not much.

E-b0926a70bf.text: John Bagwell and I proceed to F Buoy, hooked and lost a nice spearfish. Headed south to 20 degrees north heading in 1,000 fathoms, then to C Buoy, hooked up and lost another chucker. Damn. Seen one big whitetip shark. Good time, however.

E-892885eeab.text: Birthday trip! Bagwell and I, no strikes all day.
E-892885eeab.note: Looks like there's a note here, 100 hours check by Gary of Kona Coast.

E-60a3429f31.text: Fishing with brother Kevin at 7:15, about half a mile from the harbor. On the way to the grounds, a big blue marlin hits the Kona plunger on the short starboard line and thrashes around on top as he beats the bait silly, then came unhooked and charged the shotgun line. Hooks up and proceeds to rip off line from the 80-pound Penn, breaks the line. Don’t know how, but he was big. Seven hundred pounds is what the boat next to us estimated his weight at. No strikes the rest of the day.
E-60a3429f31.note: Looks like there's a note here, 8 hours. Probably how long they were out that day.

E-a8d50b797b.text: John Bagwell and I head south and have a double hookup on striped marlin off Red Hill. One comes off after a few minutes, but I land the other one of about 60 pounds on the old 50-pound reel. It was a very good but a fast fight. We then worked inshore for wahoo down to Kona Paradise and to the lava flows, but no takers.

E-541740519b.text: John Bagwell, Maddie Drew, and her sister Roz and I head south with the pretty tall following seas. Go down as far as the Double O Buoy without a strike. We switch to wahoo gear at the 1941 flow and head north toward Kealakekua Bay, Captain Cook Bay, using the Yo-Zuri Exterminator and a Huntington spoon.
E-541740519b.note:
Captain is using visual landmarks along the shore of the island for navigation because all the fishing is done within sight of the island. The 1941 flow refers to a lava flow from that year. 

Continued on the next page.

P-page-050-prefix.text:
Black with purple top. The Exterminator were orange and black tops with new stainless double tuna hooks.

We got three strikes and put two nice onos in the boat. One about 15 pounds and the other 30 pounds. We trolled about 100 yards to 50 yards offshore. Stopped at Kealakekua Bay to take pictures and look around. It’s a beautiful, beautiful place, very unchanged from when Captain Cook was here.

E-0857b1d262.text: John Bagwell and I work a porpoise school five miles west of the C Buoy, and catch some nice yellowfin, but there were some nice yellowfin were being caught, but can’t get one to hit. Then we head toward UU Buoy, and on the way I got a nice 45-pound shortbill spearfish on a Penn 50 using a Yo-Zuri pearl head with a yellow and blue skirt. That’s the second shortbill for that lure in addition to a striped marlin.
E-0857b1d262.note: A lot of the fishing around the Kona Coast revolves around buoys and other objects on the surface that tend to attract fish. It's too deep out there for rigs, which form artificial reefs on the Gulf Cost, so a big object at the top anchored by a long chain does more or less the same thing.

E-a89b2ac022.text: Joy Mickelson, Michael and Alex and I head south. No strike all day, no porpoise and only a few birds.

E-6f1cb886fd.text:
John Bagwell and I head for C Buoy. On the way, we see a cluster of skiffs about three miles offshore between VV and C Buoy, lots of porpoise leaping out of the water, chasing flying fish in all directions. Handliners were doing well, but not us sports. The ahi were down deep.

We headed for F Buoy because Captain Tom Seibler said that he caught a few mahi off of a floater nearby (that’s floating seaweed). We found it after three other boats did, but it still held a big school of small ahi and aku. We rigged for marlin on the 130s and continued to troll King Kings and caught another 10-pound shibi and the five- to 10-pound class. Ten of them.

It was now four o’clock and we were bringing in the lines when a big whitetip shark hit the aku on the port long rigger. He came in pretty quick, about a 250-pounder, and we let him cut through the leader at the boat. Big ugly critter. I was taking pictures of him and he really threw his jaws out at me. I didn’t think much of him until then!

E-a73bd50f4b.text: First blue marlin landed on the Seahawk, 287-pounder. Not a monster, but good enough for openers. My poor gaff job probably is what kept him from going over 300 pounds.

E-428706f871.text:
We started out trolling from the harbor to VV Buoy, then headed inshore to Red Hill, where we switched to wahoo gear and worked the 50- to 100-fathom curve all the way down to the Lump Dick lava flow, about 16 miles. No hits.

We then trolled out to UV Buoy, about three miles, and put out King Kings for aku. Captain Brian called to say that he was making baits nearby, and in short order we found the school. Mike caught one aku and then two small ahi. We rigged up the four-pound aku and a 10-pound ahi for trollers and headed offshore. Mike caught another yellowfin for food. Mike called his bait fish Rover.

Mike was sitting forward on the console cooler, working on his vocabulary lessons, and asked me a question. So I left the wheel to John and was sitting next to Michael when John noticed the port rigger rubber band stretching to about two feet. He hauled down the lanyard, popped the band, and the bait dropped back, and then he free-spooled it. He hollered for me to floorboard the boat when he said so. He did and I did, and we were hooked up.

About a 30-minute fight, and he came in green. I had a good fly gaff shot at him but hit him low and a bit aft of his right pectoral. All hell broke loose, and he is on top with that one-inch rope tight as a fiddle string. Quite a sight, a lot of water being thrown. I loaded the new .410-gauge Snake Charmer shotgun and settled his hash as he surfaced on the starboard side. Until then, he was pulling our old Seahawk around at a speed of two to three knots.
E-428706f871.note:
Continued from the previous page and on the next page. 

A fly gaff is a big-game fishing tool with a detachable hook head tied to a long rope rather than permanently fixed to a pole. Once the hook is driven into a large fish, the pole detaches so the crew can control and tire the fish using the rope secured to the boat.

P-page-053-prefix.text:
Then the job of getting him in the boat. It took four attempts with five-minute rests to finally get him in the boat. Son Michael was tending Rover forward on the starboard side, but he listened to us, and the only way we got him into the boat was getting Mike in the act. His 150 pounds made the difference. We pulled out the fighting chair to make room for the marlin in the cockpit.

We trolled back into Kona without another strike, but wow, what a day. Tim and Linda married today. What a great time to be alive.
P-page-053-prefix.note:
Continued from the previous pages. 

There's a note from me, Mike, here that says: My opinion is that was some ass-whoopin fish. I was up in the bow when it happened with Rover. The marlin was so close to the tuna I was holding I almost fainted.

E-f22aa9626b.text: John and I cover lots of ground, not one strike. The vog was horrible. I’ve never seen it so thick. From VV, I could not even see Kona. My eyes were watering. The further south you went, the worse it became.
E-f22aa9626b.note: Vog is what locals call the smokey air that comes from the volcano. The south point of the Big Island is where the volcano is most active.

E-c32ebb40a4.text:
John, Dr. Groom and I head for F Buoy, find a floater, and collect one ono. No one else home. We then had two fish on, probably striped marlin, and pulled both loose.

Headed south to the U Buoy, came outside of the buoy about three miles and hit a good rip and followed it to the Limpdick Man area. Hit a nice 42-pound spearfish and then a few minutes later a good 50-pound striped marlin. Jed caught all three. He’s been a good doctor to us here, and I was glad to return the favors. First two-billfish day on the Seahawk, first three-flag day.

E-9e47e109c9.text:
We fished south to 16 degrees. If not to South Point, it will have to do. Went after ono, which is wahoo, and got five hits and two in the boat. Michael caught them both. He’s had a good week. He won the science and English medal for the sixth and seventh grade at Parker, and now he catches his first wahoo.

Gary does the first one-hour servicing of the engines at the Kona Coast Marine. All is well.

E-2929b191c0.text: Mike, Alex, John Bagwell, and I head south to VV Buoy. Lots of bait, the most aku I’ve seen this year. We catch a few and rig for bait. While one is swimming along the port side, something hits him and takes out lots of 130-pound line before spitting it out. We caught 12 aku and shibi, saw a nice pod of pilot whales, big bulbous-headed, ill-tempered brutes.
E-2929b191c0.note: Shibi is Hawaiian slang for a small yellowfin tuna.

E-page-054-june-10.text: What a bummer. John and I go north to OTEC, work the porpoise schools for hours, only one strike. Engine trouble also. Starboard starts making a clicking sound. Cut it and proceed to troll home on port engine at eight knots. I’m still in warranty, thank God.

E-39d20371d1.text:
Fish with John three times with Bill Peace, Chris, and son Mike. Two nights one day, no fish. Break off an ahi. 

A little seahorse is found in the 'chute. After night of fishlessness only catch!
E-39d20371d1.note: Captain Ed: we put a parachute out at night as a drag, as we drift for ahi, and all we caught was that little seahorse.

E-86dff91ead.text: To heck with waiting around for a new powerhead. I want to go out in my own boat, so Scott and Joan Hill and I do that. Catch some aku for bait and nail a 173-pound yellowfin tuna at VV?, a real beauty. Joan is in the chair for one hour, five minutes on the port Penn 130. Scott wired and I gaffed, and we brought him in with the come-along.
E-86dff91ead.note: That was a beautiful yellowfin tuna. We have a picture we’ll include.

E-6507298e3d.text: Scott and I motor out to VV again on one engine. Only fish caught were aku for bait. One time south of VV, two baits get nervous, but no takers.

E-e50fe93880.text: Patricia, Mary Lynn Woodall, and Kay Hart go with me for a midday run down the coast to the Captain Cook Monument, then back to VV for a try at catching some aku for bait. Three on, but bad porpoise gets them all.

E-d4d686153b.text:
Jed Groom and I fish the grounds. We drug a live aku around for five hours and no luck. We did get a good hit on the Yo-Zuri jet head, ripped out a bunch of line on the 80-pound rig, spit out the hook.

We ended the day by catching 15 aku, and four of them in the 10-pound range for sashimi. Good fun. We watched a 400-pound marlin being caught by another boat. Almost jumped in our boat. Beautiful fish.

E-7d68091d9c.text:
Earl and I leave Konakahou Harbor at 6 a.m. and head to VV, catch a 25-pound wahoo on the Yo-Zuri jet head. This lure has now caught two chuckers, two stripes, and this wahoo. Went as far south as [Kaki’s Point?]. Had three other ono strikes, but none stuck.

Picked up and ran 27 knots back to VV to be there for the expected ahi. We had one on and lost him, caught four aku for sashimi.

E-ab4feb3cdc.text: Patricia Tyler, Patrick Fleming, and son Mike on board. VV Buoy. We lost the starboard engine. Caught a boatload of aku. Good time.

E-1d25cc3a05.text: Patricia, Mike, and I. More of the same.

E-6842a8dba4.text: Fish on the Deceiver with Mike and Patrick. Caught four tombos. Boys each get a 55-pound-class tombo.

E-e3af3da105.text: Mike and I fish with Captain Scott Pruner on the Deceiver. Two 400-plus-pound tombos at 5 a.m. Earl and I fish south, one nice otado, 20 pounds or so. Marlin hooked up, probably a striped one, on and off in 30 minutes.

E-d5db7613a2.text: Tad, David fish with me and their wives. One small shibi at F Buoy.

E-a6c4694b24.text: Earl, Britt and I, we go to F Buoy, chum up three nice mahi-mahi in the 15- to 25-pound class. Have another breakoff.

E-bf6a6be307.text: Sister Missy, Mike Gillespie and I. Quick trip to F Buoy, no one home, right back to the harbor, rough seas.

E-7140ba2c2b.text: John Bagwell and I lose port engine at the grounds, lose a marlin at 5:15 on a live aku.

E-050cd32b01.text: Beautiful day, I go out by myself. Very exciting, but no strikes. I was very careful, but I felt really free and all senses were at 100%. Eight-hour trip.

E-fb8b244815.text: Tom [Seaver?] and I, same deal. No birds, no bait, no strikes.

E-3200718613.text: Son Mike Fleming and I go to [Honokōhau?], the grounds, the F Buoy and VV. No luck, quit at 2 o’clock.

E-d347903c6a.text: Drew Van Quillen, Mike and I. Drew gets sick, so I take him and Michael back to the harbor. Then I go by myself north along the 50-fathom curve, catch two nice wahoo, 15 and 30 pounds, on heavy jet head, red, white and blue.

E-f9e843059b.text: John Bagwell and I go to the grounds, one hit on live bait. It’s a wahoo as it cut the Dacron harness. Slow.

E-17463f0181.text: Fish with Robin Cipriano, a fellow Mako owner whose boat was in the shop. I invited him to go with me. Great visit, no strikes.

E-272645e091.text: Guy Cellier and Mario on board. We head to the grounds and look for bait trolling King Kings. Hit a big otado. He in turn is hit by Bent Fin himself. He fought on a 40-pound line for over an hour, finally spitting out a three- to four-pound head. Could have shot the rascal several times. One wahoo hit, then back to port.
E-272645e091.note: Bent Fin was a resident dolphin in the area named for having an identifiable bent dorsal fin. It was notorious for stealing live bait and sometimes even a catch. Shooting him would have put ol' Ed in trouble with the feds as it would have been a violation of the Marine Mammals Protection Act of 1972.

E-849f8765a4.text: Reagan Matsumura on board. Leave south off of Red Hill, lots of bait up on the ledge. Got a marlin hit on the big blue-purple soft head. Hit the leader two foot above the lure, out of the clip, but no hookup. Only hit for the day.

E-acca5d3859.text: Doug Seymour and John Bagwell on board. We go to F Buoy, lots of bait, no predators.

E-2831b6e9d0.text: Doug shows me a snapper spot off of OTEC that was really good. We caught 21 bright red fish, red snapper, in about one hour, commencing about 10 a.m. One grouper-looking, looking fellow, purple with yellow and black spots, of about five pounds also taken.

E-1c97b030c4.text: Trolled the grounds out to F Buoy, Red Hill with Doug Seymour. No strikes, nice day. One snapper on a drift by light south of the harbor.

E-e3581660fb.text: Earl Regador, Doug Seymour on board. We went to F Buoy and trolling purple jet heads, no luck. Turned north and ran to the edge of the grounds, back to the OTEC station, where we caught 15 onos that we’ll cook at our house this weekend. Good time.

E-bc5516df17.text: Doug Seymour and I trolled out to the grounds, tried chumming with no success. Lost an ono on a Yo-Zuri lure, ripped tail out of the skirt, and apparently lost a billfish on the troll. Dead ono.

E-417d9d7b91.text: Hooked a whale, lost him. Caught a 20-pound ahi off the Pines, Yo-Zuri lure jet head, old reliable.
E-417d9d7b91.note: Actually did run the lures across a whale accidentally and hooked into the pleated belly of a humpback as he rolled. Obviously we had to cut that one loose.

E-1897c0c4a8.text: Mike Fleming, Mike Gouveia, and his friend Gavin go with us today. We catch a small mahi-mahi right outside the jetties on a ballyhoo under a pink-blue skirt. Choppy seas. We go in by 11:30. No other strikes. Wind from the west, pretty choppy today.

E-795ee63a0a.text:
Doug Seymour and Dr. Jed Groom and I finally hit the ono at 3:30 p.m., about 150 yards north of the Pines in 40 fathoms. Both nice 35-pound-class fish. One hit the old faithful, the Yo-Zuri, and the other the reliable heavy jet ono lure with red, white, and black skirts.

The key was given to us by our new friend Jerry Kemchow, who caught four, by telling us to drop the lines back 200 to 300 feet further back than we normally do. Good day.

E-06ef66a8a7.text:
Doug Seymour and new friend Jerry [Kemchow] on board. Head south to the Miloliʻi area. In about three miles south of Miloliʻi, we get into the fish. Used waypoint 38. It is a small ledge next to a small bay that was loaded with ono. We ended up with 18 in the boat and three hit and lost. Every size. 25 to 35 pounds, with one 40-pounder.

We used the Yo-Zuri and the heavy weighted ono lures. Jerry also had some super lures that did a great job. Total trip is about 35 miles south of Honokōhau Harbor. Coordinates are 19.03.0 north and 155.54.41 west. Great trip. Doug sold most of the fish and gave me $350 in proceeds to put toward boat repairs.

E-9fc2c0c9b3.text:
Mike Fleming and three of his buddies, Ricky, Mike Gouveia, and Gavin, and Coach Kuhio, go with me to the same area as on the 9th. We fished down to the concrete platform and out about 70 fathoms. We got into the ono again as we caught seven, including a 46-pound beauty that Michael landed. Ricky hooked a 30-pound ahi, which was a nice surprise.

Big producers were the heavy brass chromed heads with red, white, and black skirts, as well as the homemade yellow and white, which landed two. We lost one lure when another ono struck the swivel after his buddy was hooked. Dark and forbidding country down there by South Point, but worth the run.

Starboard engine light comes on halfway home at 3,000 RPM. Hope it was just the filters. Gary will check that next week.
E-9fc2c0c9b3.note: We had a 100-hour checkup at the Kona Marine after this trip. Estimate 460 hours on the powerhead of the starboard engine and 820 hours on the port engine.

E-a8d20166da.text: Same place. Doug and Jerry, only three ono this time. The boat Marlin Mischief out of Hanoi runs alongside us as we approach Miloliʻi on the way back and gave us a 125- to 150-pound blue marlin, which Doug will have in the smoker tomorrow. Great day.

E-c8b8aa209e.text:
Doug Seymour, Jerry Kemchow on board. We gear up and head for Miloliʻi?, leaving the harbor at 8:45 a.m. Seas nice and calm, wind south-southwest. The skies were clear as the Kona wind blew out the vog down south. Beautiful run at 21 knots.

We put the baits out at Pinnacle Rock, about one mile north of Miloliʻi?. We caught a nice 38-pound ono there and lost another before heading down further south to waypoint number 38. We put four more good ono in the box before heading back north at 1:30 p.m. as the seas were roughing up a bit.

Four of the five onos were caught on the mahi-colored Marauder that I had rigged with a single number 10 hook. I ran them off the corner at 7.5 knots, and they were great. The strikes are fierce on these things.

We stuck to our game plan and headed straight out 270 degrees off Miloliʻi to where we think the 2,000-fathom line is, then turned north to troll home. Bait and birds showing up, as well as nice slicks. Soon saw the starboard outrigger 130 go off, and we have a nice striped marlin on and kept him. Doug gets in the chair, Jerry drives, and I gaff, leader and gaff and shoot. All works fine. 125-pound marlin. Good trip.

Starboard engine seems a bit starved for fuel, lost power twice during the trip, then it would throttle up and be okay.

42 fish last eight trips!
E-c8b8aa209e.note: There’s a sketch below the map showing Kona Paradise, the Limp Dick Man lava formation, Miloliʻi, Pinnacle Rock, and the VV buoy, which we ought to include in our maps.

E-4cbc02d240.text:
Doug Seymour and son Daniel and I worked the 50-fathom curve line north to the grounds. Then we, at Top Corner and to the top corner and back, caught three aku and harnessed them up, one in the downrigger 200 feet and his buddy on the starboard outrigger. Rigged a dead ono on the port outrigger as a splash bait. It was a fine-looking rig.

No known hits. However, when we reeled in the rig for ono, we discovered that the starboard aku was cleanly cut in two. A big ono would be my guess, but it could have been a shark. The downrigger aku was live, but looked like he had taken a wrap.

We then ran two Marauders off the corners and two heavy chrome heads off the riggers about 300 feet back. A 25-pound ono hit the orange Marauder and became young Daniel’s first ono and biggest fish.

John Price tells me this morning to have Gary check the fuel pump on the starboard engine. All symptoms to him sound like that’s the problem. The pump works well enough at low speed, but at some high RPMs it can’t supply what the injector pumps need. Also said to be sure Gary sprays and decarbonizes the cylinders every 50 hours. Use full can per engine. Lord, it’s great to have a good mechanic friend in Port Aransas can advise our local boys what to do.
